script: Fired from my job, but received a years worth of pay and got my Boss fired.. The early 2010s was when I got hired as a content creator for a university. They wanted to splash their name on YouTube and thought a single dude could make it happen. I got a paycheck of about $2200 a month and a stack of old gear that barely did 720p. But here's the thing: on day two, my manager slid me a KPI sheet that said 85 videos of 3‑10 minutes each in a year. I stared, because that was a one‑man army nightmare. What I didn't know was how tight their expectations were, and that I had to script, cast, shoot, edit, and even compose music myself. The manager smiled, said "give it a try, quality over quantity." I nodded, feeling the heat of that promise. However, the next week, she found out I smoked. Suddenly, her face flipped. She started nitpicking my every move: cigarette smell, 5‑minute late arrivals, not answering texts during breaks. I kept working, because I wanted the videos to shine, not because I wanted to be her pet. Until, one day, she called me into the Director's office. In that cramped room, I felt my stomach drop. The director was disappointed because I had only finished 30 out of 85 videos in the first half of the year. He said, "The KPI is 85. We need to fire you if you can't meet it." I tried to explain the grind: 60+ hours a week, my own equipment, and the videos I posted had the highest views on their channel. But he shrugged, saying they could hire a production house. That's when a lightbulb flickered. The manager laughed, "We'll find a professional house to finish the job." The director looked at her, then at me, and said, "You don't need to worry, manager will get the job done." I thought, "Oh, this is it." I remembered my database of production houses—my one job in the office was to keep that list up to date. I changed all the contacts except one. I called my friend who was a junior director at a small house. I pitched the plan: he gets a big win, I get a 15% finder's fee. He said yes, and the next day they signed a contract for a six‑month project, a high‑six‑digit payout. They were the perfect fit. They understood the university's vibe and could produce a video every two to three days. So, in four months, they churned out 50 videos, costing them double to triple my monthly salary. I sat back and collected 15% of that—about 15 months of my salary. I used the money for a holiday in Bali and paid for a film school overseas. But here's the thing: that was only the beginning. While I was sipping coconut on a beach, my colleague—who had face‑palmed me when I told her about the smoking issue—called. She said the former manager had been fired and the director was getting a massive blow from the Chancellor. The content project, which had been budgeted for about a year and a half of my salary, had blown the budget ten times over. The manager had spent whatever she could to keep the project alive, ignoring the director's authority. The Chancellor was furious and the university had to make a statement. The call left me stunned. What I didn't know was that the whole fiasco had been a ripple. The university's board had been watching me, and my success was proving the manager's incompetence. They had decided to fire her and punish the director for letting the budget spiral. And that's when everything changed: my little scheme had not only paid off but also toppled the wrong people. I felt a rush of satisfaction, because I was better than the people in the story. But here's the thing: the story was far from over, and the final chapter was still unwritten.
